opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and I think it's one of the central challenges for embodied AI right now.

For a long time, robotics was very task-specific. You'd build one system to pick up boxes in a warehouse, another to weld car parts, another to vacuum the floor, and each had its own perception module, its own control policy, its own data. None of that knowledge transferred. Every new task meant starting almost from scratch, which is why robotics scaled so much more slowly than, say, language models.

What's changed is that we now have foundation models. Large language models and vision-language models already contain a huge amount of general knowledge about the world: what objects are, how they relate, what people mean when they give an instruction. So the first layer of shared intelligence should be this common "brain": a general model of semantics, reasoning, and planning that every robot can draw on, regardless of its specific job.

The second layer is what I'd call shared physical intelligence. Robots need to understand physics: friction, force, how a cup behaves differently from a towel. That knowledge is common across grasping, assembly, cooking, and folding laundry. If we can train vision-language-action models on diverse data from many tasks and many different robot bodies, the model learns representations that generalize. We've seen early evidence that training across embodiments actually makes each individual robot better, not worse.

Third, there's the question of how robots share experience with each other. A human learns individually, and it takes years. But robots can, in principle, pool what they learn. If one robot in a factory figures out how to handle a tricky part, that experience can be uploaded, distilled, and shared with thousands of others. That's a kind of collective learning that biology doesn't allow, and I think it's one of the most powerful advantages machines have.

Of course, there are real challenges. Data is the biggest one. Unlike text on the internet, there's no massive natural corpus of robot actions. So we need a combination of simulation, human demonstration video, teleoperation, and real-world deployment data, and we need ways to bridge the gap between simulation and reality.

There's also the architecture question. I tend to think the answer is a hierarchical system: a large general model for high-level understanding and planning, combined with smaller, faster, more specialized modules at the edge for real-time control. You don't want a giant model in the cloud deciding every millisecond of motor movement, but you do want it guiding the overall behavior.

Finally, safety has to be shared too. As intelligence becomes more general and more transferable, a mistake or vulnerability can also propagate. So the shared layer has to include shared safety constraints and alignment, so that robots don't just get more capable together but also remain reliable and trustworthy together.

So my short answer is a common foundation model as the brain, shared physical representations learned across tasks and bodies, collective learning from fleets of robots, and a hierarchical design that balances generality with real-time specialization. That's the direction I think will take robotics from single-purpose machines toward genuinely general-purpose physical intelligence.

r001.rationale: It proposes a common foundation model that every robot can draw on regardless of its specific job, and describes robots pooling and sharing learned experience.

r002.rationale: It presents a general model of semantics, reasoning, and planning as a shared foundation, then describes learning physical skills across tasks and robot bodies.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because it really gets at what embodied intelligence is versus what traditional robotics was. In the old paradigm, you'd build a robot for one task — welding, or picking a specific part off a specific conveyor — and the intelligence was essentially hard-coded and task-specific. Nothing transferred. If you wanted the same arm to do something slightly different, you basically started over.

What's changed is the foundation model paradigm. The lesson from large language models is that you don't train a model for translation, and another for summarization, and another for coding. You train one model on a huge, diverse corpus, and the capabilities emerge and transfer. I think robots will follow a similar path, with one important difference: the data isn't sitting on the internet waiting to be scraped. Physical interaction data has to be generated.

So the way I think about sharing intelligence across tasks is in layers. At the top, you have a general model that understands the world — language, vision, physics, common sense about objects and spaces. That layer should be shared across essentially everything, whether it's a humanoid, a quadruped, or a robotic arm. It's what lets a robot understand "put the cup on the shelf" without having been trained on that exact cup or that exact shelf.

Below that, you have a layer that maps from that understanding to action. And here the key idea is that skills should be composable. Grasping, moving, placing, navigating — these primitives shouldn't belong to one task. If the robot learns to grasp a deformable object while folding laundry, that same skill should be available when it's packing a box. The way you get there is by training across many tasks simultaneously, so the representation the model learns is about the underlying physics and affordances rather than about the task label.

Then at the bottom, there's the embodiment-specific part — the control of that particular body, its joints, its sensors. This will vary across hardware, and it's probably the least shareable, though even here I think we'll see more cross-embodiment transfer than people expect.

The thing I'd emphasize is that this requires a different relationship between simulation and real-world data. You can't collect enough real robot hours to cover every task. So simulation, synthetic data, and video from humans doing things become the bridge. The model learns the general structure of tasks in a cheap, scalable way, and then real-world data refines it. That's how intelligence gets amortized across tasks instead of rebuilt for each one.

And honestly, I think the sharing goes beyond individual robots. If one robot learns something in a warehouse in Shenzhen, that experience should improve the model that every robot runs. It's a fleet learning problem. That's where the economics become compelling, because the cost of each new task approaches zero while the capability keeps compounding.

r001.rationale: The response proposes a general model shared across tasks and robot types, with fleet learning allowing one robot’s experience to improve the model used by others.

r002.rationale: It describes a shared foundation that understands the world, including common sense about objects and spaces, and maps that understanding to task skills.

astra-6.text:
I think robots should share a common foundation of intelligence, while developing specialized capabilities for different tasks. A robot working in a kitchen and a robot working in a factory both need to understand objects, space, motion, and the consequences of their actions. They should be able to build on that shared knowledge rather than learn everything from scratch.

But sharing intelligence does not mean copying behavior directly. Different robots have different bodies, sensors, and operating environments. Knowledge has to be adapted to those differences. Knowing how to grasp an object is useful across many tasks; knowing how much force to apply depends on the object and the robot.

The opportunity is to make learning cumulative: experience from one task helps improve performance on another. The challenge is making sure that what transfers is actually useful and safe.

r001.rationale: The response says robots should share a common foundation of intelligence across tasks.

r002.rationale: It describes shared knowledge about objects, space, motion, and consequences as a basis for developing specialized capabilities for different tasks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think robots should share a common foundation of intelligence, while developing specialized skills for different tasks. Understanding the physical world, recognizing objects, planning actions—those capabilities should transfer. A robot shouldn’t have to learn everything from scratch when it moves from one task to another.

But sharing intelligence doesn’t mean copying the same movement everywhere. Different robots have different bodies, sensors, and operating environments. So you need a shared model that captures general knowledge, combined with adaptation to the particular robot and task.

The exciting possibility is that experience can benefit the whole system. If one robot learns something useful, others can build on it. The challenge is making sure that what transfers is reliable and appropriate, especially when robots act around people.

r001.rationale: It proposes a shared model of general knowledge and intelligence that can transfer across robots and tasks.

r002.rationale: It presents general capabilities such as understanding the physical world, recognizing objects, and planning as a foundation for task-specific skills.
